title: Wisdom

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 1
summaryBullets: Love righteousness, you rulers of the earth; think of the Lord in goodness and seek him with sincerity of heart, (1:1).
because he is found by those who do not put him to the test and manifests himself to those who do not distrust him. (1:2).
For perverse thoughts separate people from God, and when his power is tested, it exposes the foolish, (1:3).
because wisdom will not enter a deceitful soul or dwell in a body enslaved to sin. (1:4).
For a holy and disciplined spirit will flee from deceit and will leave foolish thoughts behind and will be ashamed at the approach of unrighteousness. (1:5).

For wisdom is a kindly spirit, but it will not free blasphemers from the guilt of their words, because God is witness of their inmost feelings and a true observer of their hearts and a hearer of their tongues. (1:6).
Because the spirit of the Lord has filled the world and that which holds all things together knows what is said, (1:7).
therefore those who utter unrighteous things will not escape notice, and justice, when it punishes, will not pass them by. (1:8).
For inquiry will be made into the counsels of the ungodly, and a report of their words will come to the Lord, to convict them of their lawless deeds, (1:9).
because a jealous ear hears all things, and the sound of grumbling does not go unheard. (1:10).
Beware, then, of useless grumbling, and keep your tongue from slander, because no secret word is without result, and a lying mouth destroys the soul. (1:11).
Do not court death by the error of your life or bring on destruction by the works of your hands, (1:12).
because God did not make death, and he does not delight in the destruction of the living. (1:13).
For he created all things so that they might exist; the generative forces of the world are wholesome, and there is no destructive poison in them, and the dominion of Hades is not on earth. (1:14).
For righteousness is immortal. (1:15).
But the ungodly by their words and deeds summoned death; considering him a friend, they pined away and made a covenant with him, because they are fit to belong to his company. (1:16).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 28:9: Seek the Lord with a whole heart, for He searches every thought and plan.
Psalm 139:7-12: No place hides a person from the Spirit of the Lord.
Ezekiel 18:32: God takes no pleasure in the death of anyone who dies.
Isaiah 28:15: Men boast of a covenant made with death and an agreement with Sheol.
Matthew 12:36: An account will be given on the day of judgment for every careless word.

translationNotes.note: Haplotes means single-fold or undivided, the opposite of duplicity. The phrase describes a person acting from one motive rather than keeping a second, hidden one in reserve.

translationNotes.term: that which holds all things together
translationNotes.original: Greek: τὸ συνέχον τὰ πάντα (to synechon ta panta)
translationNotes.note: A phrase from Greek natural philosophy for whatever binds the cosmos into one working whole. The book is written in Greek for Greek-speaking readers and uses their vocabulary for the world.
Muttered complaint made under the breath rather than open protest. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel's murmuring in the wilderness at Exodus 16:7-9.
The realm of the dead. Greek-speaking Jews used hades to render Hebrew Sheol, the place where the dead are gathered; in pagan Greek it named the underworld and the god who ruled it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Solomon calls the rulers of the earth to love righteousness and seek the Lord sincerely, since wisdom will not enter a deceitful soul. The spirit of the Lord fills the world and hears every word, God did not make death, and the ungodly summoned it and made a covenant with it.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 2
summaryBullets: For they reasoned unsoundly, saying to themselves, “Short and sorrowful is our life, and there is no remedy when a life comes to its end, and no one has been known to return from Hades. (2:1).
For we were born by mere chance, and hereafter we shall be as though we had never been, for the breath in our nostrils is smoke, and reason is a spark kindled by the beating of our hearts; (2:2).
when it is extinguished, the body will turn to ashes, and the spirit will dissolve like empty air. (2:3).

Our name will be forgotten in time, and no one will remember our works; our life will pass away like the traces of a cloud and be scattered like mist that is chased by the rays of the sun and overcome by its heat. (2:4).
For our allotted time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no return from our death, because it is sealed up and no one turns back. (2:5).
“Come, therefore, let us enjoy the good things that exist and make use of the creation to the full as in youth. (2:6).
Let us take our fill of costly wine and perfumes, and let no flower of spring pass us by. (2:7).
Let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they wither. (2:8).
Let no meadow be free from our revelry; everywhere let us leave signs of enjoyment, because this is our portion, and this our lot. (2:9).
Let us oppress the righteous poor man; let us not spare the widow or regard the gray hairs of the aged. (2:10).
But let our might be our law of right, for what is weak proves itself to be useless. (2:11).
“Let us lie in wait for the righteous man, because he is inconvenient to us and opposes our actions; he reproaches us for sins against the law and accuses us of sins against our training. (2:12).
He professes to have knowledge of God and calls himself a child of the Lord. (2:13).
He became to us a reproof of our thoughts; the very sight of him is a burden to us, (2:14).
because his manner of life is unlike that of others, and his ways are strange. (2:15).
We are considered by him as something base, and he avoids our ways as unclean; he calls the last end of the righteous happy and boasts that God is his father. (2:16).
Let us see if his words are true, and let us test what will happen at the end of his life, (2:17).
for if the righteous man is God’s child, he will help him and will deliver him from the hand of his adversaries. (2:18).
Let us test him with insult and torture, so that we may find out how reasonable he is and make trial of his forbearance. (2:19).
Let us condemn him to a shameful death, for, according to what he says, he will be protected.” (2:20).
Thus they reasoned, but they were led astray, for their wickedness blinded them, (2:21).
and they did not know the secret purposes of God, nor hoped for the wages of holiness, nor discerned the prize for blameless souls, (2:22).
for God created us for incorruption and made us in the image of his own eternity, (2:23).
but through an adversary’s envy death entered the world, and those who belong to his company experience it. (2:24).
crossRefs: Isaiah 22:13: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.
Amos 2:6-7: They trample the head of the poor and push the afflicted out of the way.
Psalm 22:8: He trusted in the Lord; let Him rescue him, since He delights in him.
Matthew 27:43: He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, for he said, I am the Son of God.
Genesis 3:1-6: The counsel of the serpent and the eating that brought death in.

translationNotes.note: The adverb means offhand, improvised, made up on the spot. It describes something thrown together without plan rather than something merely unlucky.

translationNotes.original: Greek: στεψώμεθα ῥόδων κάλυξιν (stepsometha rhodon kalyxin)
translationNotes.note: Guests at a Greek banquet wore woven garlands of flowers on the head, and the host provided them along with the wine and perfume. The image is the drinking party, not a coronation.
The state of not decaying, freedom from the corruption that overtakes bodies and things. Paul uses the same word repeatedly in 1 Corinthians 15:42-54.
Diabolos means slanderer or accuser, one who throws a charge across at another. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the accuser in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3, and English devil comes from it.

stories.keyTakeaway: The ungodly reason that life is short and ends in nothing, so they seize pleasure, oppress the poor and the widow, and make might their law. They plot insult, torture, and a shameful death for the righteous man who calls God his father, blind to the incorruption God made them for.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 3
summaryBullets: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them. (3:1).
In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died, and their departure was thought to be a disaster (3:2).
and their going from us to be their destruction, but they are at peace. (3:3).
For though in the sight of others they were punished, their hope is full of immortality. (3:4).
Having been disciplined a little, they will receive great good, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself; (3:5).
like gold in the furnace he tried them, and like a sacrificial burnt offering he accepted them. (3:6).
In the time of their visitation they will shine forth and will run like sparks through the stubble. (3:7).
They will govern nations and rule over peoples, and the Lord will reign over them forever. (3:8).
Those who trust in him will understand truth, and the faithful will abide with him in love, because grace and mercy are upon his holy ones, and he watches over his elect. (3:9).
But the ungodly will be punished as their reasoning deserves, those who disregarded the righteous and rebelled against the Lord, (3:10).
for those who despise wisdom and instruction are miserable. Their hope is vain, their labors are unprofitable, and their works are useless. (3:11).
Their wives are foolish and their children evil; their offspring are accursed. (3:12).
For blessed is the barren woman who is undefiled, who has not entered into a sinful union; she will have fruit when God examines souls. (3:13).

Blessed also is the eunuch whose hands have done no lawless deed and who has not devised wicked things against the Lord, for special favor will be shown him for his faithfulness and a place of great delight in the temple of the Lord. (3:14).
For the fruit of good labors is renowned, and the root of understanding does not fail. (3:15).
But children of adulterers will not come to maturity, and the offspring of an unlawful union will perish. (3:16).
Even if they live long they will be held of no account, and finally their old age will be without honor. (3:17).
If they die young, they will have no hope and no consolation on the day of judgment. (3:18).
For the end of an unrighteous generation is grievous. (3:19).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 33:3: All His holy ones are in His hand.
Malachi 3:2-3: He sits as a refiner and purifier of silver.
Daniel 12:3: The wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky.
Isaiah 54:1: Sing, O barren one who did not bear.
Isaiah 56:3-5: The eunuch who keeps God's covenant is given a name better than sons and daughters.

translationNotes.note: Psyche covers the life, breath, and self of a person, the whole living being. In the Greek Old Testament it renders Hebrew nephesh, which is used of animals and people alike.
Built from a- (not) and thanatos (death), so literally deathlessness. It was a standing term in Greek writing for existence that does not end, and the book uses it rather than a word for long life.
An overseeing or inspection, the moment a superior comes to look over what is his and settle accounts. The same root gives episkopos, overseer, from which English gets bishop.
A castrated male, commonly a household or palace officer in the ancient Near East, often set over the women's quarters or the treasury. Deuteronomy 23:1 barred such a man from the assembly.

stories.keyTakeaway: The souls of the righteous are in God's hand; they only seemed to die, and their hope is full of immortality. Tried like gold in a furnace, they will shine forth and govern nations, while the ungodly get what their reasoning deserves and the undefiled barren woman and eunuch are called blessed.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 4
summaryBullets: Better than this is childlessness with virtue, for in the memory of virtue is immortality, because it is known both by God and by mortals. (4:1).
When it is present, people imitate it, and they long for it when it has gone; throughout all time it marches, crowned in triumph, victor in the contest for prizes that are undefiled. (4:2).
But the prolific brood of the ungodly will be of no use, and none of their illegitimate seedlings will strike a deep root or take a firm hold. (4:3).
For even if they put forth boughs for a while, standing insecurely they will be shaken by the wind, and by the violence of the winds they will be uprooted. (4:4).
The branches will be broken off before they come to maturity, and their fruit will be useless, not ripe enough to eat and good for nothing. (4:5).
For children born of unlawful unions are witnesses of evil against their parents when God examines them. (4:6).
But the righteous, even if they die early, will be at rest. (4:7).
For old age is not honored for length of time or measured by number of years, (4:8).
but understanding is gray hair for anyone, and a blameless life is ripe old age. (4:9).
There was one who pleased God and was loved by him and while living among sinners was taken up. (4:10).
He was caught up so that evil might not change his understanding or guile deceive his soul. (4:11).
For the fascination of wickedness obscures what is good, and roving desire perverts the innocent mind. (4:12).
Being perfected in a short time, he fulfilled long years, (4:13).
for his soul was pleasing to the Lord; therefore he hastened him from the midst of wickedness. Yet the peoples saw and did not understand or take such a thing to heart, (4:14).
that God’s grace and mercy are with his elect and that he watches over his holy ones. (4:15).
The righteous who have died will condemn the ungodly who are living, and youth that is quickly perfected will condemn the prolonged old age of the unrighteous. (4:16).
For they will see the end of the wise and will not understand what the Lord purposed for them and for what he kept them safe. (4:17).
The unrighteous will see and will have contempt for them, but the Lord will laugh them to scorn. (4:18).

After this they will become dishonored corpses and an outrage among the dead forever, because he will dash them speechless to the ground and shake them from the foundations; they will be left utterly dry and barren, and they will suffer anguish, and the memory of them will perish. (4:19).
They will come with dread when their sins are reckoned up, and their lawless deeds will convict them to their face. (4:20).
crossRefs: Genesis 5:24: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.
Hebrews 11:5: By faith Enoch was taken up so that he did not see death.
Isaiah 57:1-2: The righteous perish and no one takes it to heart; they enter into peace.
Proverbs 16:31: Gray hair is a crown of glory, gained in a righteous life.
Psalm 1:3-4: The tree planted by streams of water and the chaff the wind drives away.

translationNotes.term: crowned in triumph, victor in the contest
translationNotes.note: Language from the Greek games. The agon was the contest itself, and the stephanos was the woven wreath handed to the winner, a victor's prize rather than a royal crown.
A nothos was a child born outside a lawful marriage. Under Greek city law he had no claim on his father's household, inheritance, or citizenship, so the term marks legal standing.

translationNotes.term: was taken up, was caught up
translationNotes.note: Metatithemi means to transfer or remove from one place to another, and it is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses at Genesis 5:24. Harpazo means to snatch suddenly, seizing without warning.
Gray hair was the visible proof of an elder, and elders held standing at the gate and in the assembly. The verse moves that mark from the number of years to understanding.

stories.keyTakeaway: Childlessness with virtue outlasts the brood of the ungodly, whose branches break before they ripen. The righteous who die early are at rest, since old age is measured by understanding, not years. One who pleased God was taken up from among sinners, and the peoples saw it and did not understand.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 5
summaryBullets: Then the righteous will stand with great confidence in the presence of those who have oppressed them and those who make light of their labors. (5:1).
When the unrighteous see them, they will be shaken with dreadful fear, and they will be amazed at the unexpected salvation of the righteous. (5:2).
They will speak to one another in repentance, and in anguish of spirit they will groan, (5:3).
“These are persons whom we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach—fools that we were! We thought that their lives were madness and that their end was without honor. (5:4).
Why have they been numbered among the children of God? And why is their lot among the holy ones? (5:5).
So it was we who strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine on us, and the sun did not rise upon us. (5:6).
We took our fill of the paths of lawlessness and destruction, and we journeyed through trackless deserts, but the way of the Lord we have not known. (5:7).
What has our arrogance profited us? And what good has our boasted wealth brought us? (5:8).
“All those things have vanished like a shadow and like a rumor that passes by; (5:9).
like a ship that sails through the billowy water, and when it has passed no trace can be found, no track of its keel in the waves; (5:10).

or as, when a bird flies through the air, no evidence of its passage is found; the light air, lashed by the beat of its pinions and pierced by the force of its rushing flight, is traversed by the movement of its wings, and afterward no sign of its coming is found there; (5:11).
or as, when an arrow is shot at a target, the air, thus divided, comes together at once, so that no one knows its pathway. (5:12).
So we also, as soon as we were born, ceased to be, and we had no sign of virtue to show but were consumed in our wickedness.” (5:13).

Because the hope of the ungodly is like thistledown carried by the wind and like a light frost driven away by a storm; it is dispersed like smoke before the wind, and it passes like the remembrance of a guest who stays but a day. (5:14).
But the righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord; the Most High takes care of them. (5:15).
Therefore they will receive a glorious crown and a beautiful diadem from the hand of the Lord, because with his right hand he will cover them, and with his arm he will shield them. (5:16).
The Lord will take his zeal as his whole armor and will arm all creation to repel his enemies; (5:17).
he will put on righteousness as a breastplate and wear impartial justice as a helmet; (5:18).
he will take holiness as an invincible shield (5:19).
and sharpen stern wrath for a sword, and the world will join him to fight against the senseless. (5:20).
Shafts of lightning will fly with true aim and will leap from the clouds to the target, as from a well-drawn bow, (5:21).
and hailstones full of wrath will be hurled as from a catapult; the water of the sea will rage against them, and rivers will relentlessly overwhelm them; (5:22).
a mighty wind will rise against them, and like a tempest it will winnow them away. Lawlessness will lay waste the whole earth, and evildoing will overturn the thrones of rulers. (5:23).
crossRefs: Proverbs 30:18-19: The way of an eagle in the sky and of a ship in the heart of the sea.
Psalm 1:4: The wicked are like chaff that the wind drives away.
Isaiah 59:17: He put on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation on His head.
Ephesians 6:13-17: The whole armor of God, breastplate, helmet, shield, and sword.
Joshua 10:11: Great stones from heaven fall on the enemy in the descent.

translationNotes.note: The full kit of a heavily armed infantryman: shield, helmet, breastplate, greaves, spear, and sword. Paul uses the same word for the armor of God in Ephesians 6:11.
A band of cloth tied around the head, the mark of a king in the Greek east. It is a different object from the stephanos, the woven wreath given to a victor; this verse names both together.
Literally a stone-thrower. A torsion siege engine wound with twisted cord that hurled stones against walls and massed troops, standard equipment in Hellenistic armies.

Threshed grain was tossed into the air with a fork on a high floor so the wind carried the light chaff off while the heavy grain fell back. The picture is of separation by wind, not simply scattering.

stories.keyTakeaway: The righteous stand in confidence before those who oppressed them, and the unrighteous groan, admitting their arrogance and wealth vanished like a shadow, a ship's wake, an arrow's path. The Lord crowns the righteous, then arms creation for war with breastplate, helmet, shield, and sword.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 6
summaryBullets: Listen therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, O judges of the ends of the earth. (6:1).
Give ear, you who rule over multitudes and boast of many nations. (6:2).
For your dominion was given you from the Lord and your sovereignty from the Most High; he will search out your works and inquire into your plans. (6:3).
Because as servants of his kingdom you did not rule rightly or keep the law or walk according to the purpose of God, (6:4).
he will come upon you terribly and swiftly, because severe judgment falls on those in high places. (6:5).
For the lowliest may be pardoned in mercy, but the mighty will be mightily tested. (6:6).
For the Lord of all will not stand in awe of anyone or show deference to greatness, because he himself made both small and great, and he takes thought for all alike. (6:7).
But a strict inquiry is in store for the mighty. (6:8).
To you then, O monarchs, my words are directed, so that you may learn wisdom and not transgress. (6:9).
For they will be made holy who observe holy things in holiness, and those who have been taught them will find a defense. (6:10).
Therefore set your desire on my words; long for them, and you will be instructed. (6:11).
Wisdom is radiant and unfading, and she is easily discerned by those who love her and is found by those who seek her. (6:12).
She hastens to make herself known to those who desire her. (6:13).
One who rises early to seek her will have no difficulty, for she will be found sitting at the gate. (6:14).
To fix one’s thought on her is perfect understanding, and one who is vigilant on her account will soon be free from care, (6:15).
because she goes about seeking those worthy of her, and she graciously appears to them in their paths and meets them in every thought. (6:16).
The beginning of wisdom is the most sincere desire for instruction, (6:17).
and concern for instruction is love of her, and love of her is the keeping of her laws, and giving heed to her laws is assurance of immortality, (6:18).
and immortality brings one near to God, (6:19).
so the desire for wisdom leads to a kingdom. (6:20).
Therefore if you delight in thrones and scepters, O monarchs over the peoples, honor wisdom, so that you may reign forever. (6:21).

I will tell you what wisdom is and how she came to be, and I will hide no secrets from you, but I will trace her course from the beginning of creation and make knowledge of her clear, and I will not pass by the truth, (6:22).
nor will I travel in the company of sickly envy, for envy does not associate with wisdom. (6:23).
The multitude of the wise is the salvation of the world, and a sensible king is the stability of any people. (6:24).
Therefore be instructed by my words, and you will profit. (6:25).
crossRefs: Psalm 2:10: Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth.
Romans 13:1: There is no authority except from God.
Luke 12:48: From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required.
Proverbs 8:1-3: Wisdom calls beside the gates, at the entrance of the city.

translationNotes.note: A holder of power, whether king, prince, or high officeholder. English dynasty comes from the same root, and the Greek Old Testament uses the word for any ruler with force at his command.
The city gate was the civic center: elders sat there, lawsuits were heard, contracts were witnessed, and business was done. To be found at the gate is to be available where public life happens.
Named from the amaranth flower, which keeps its color after it is cut and dried. 1 Peter 1:4 and 5:4 use the same word for an inheritance and a crown that do not wither.
The whole training of a person, education and discipline together, correction included. English translations render it as instruction, discipline, or chastening depending on context.

stories.keyTakeaway: Solomon warns kings and judges that their rule came from the Lord, who searches out their works; the lowly may be pardoned, but the mighty face strict inquiry. Wisdom is radiant and unfading, found sitting at the gate by those who rise early, and he promises to trace her course from creation.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 7
summaryBullets: I also am mortal like everyone else, a descendant of the first-formed child of earth, and in the womb of a mother I was molded into flesh, (7:1).
within the period of ten months, compacted with blood, from the seed of a man and the pleasure of marriage. (7:2).
And when I was born, I began to breathe the common air and fell upon the kindred earth; my first sound was a cry, as is true of all. (7:3).
I was nursed with care in swaddling cloths. (7:4).
For no king has had a different beginning of existence; (7:5).
there is for all one entrance into life and one way out. (7:6).
Therefore I prayed, and understanding was given me; I called on God, and the spirit of wisdom came to me. (7:7).
I preferred her to scepters and thrones, and I accounted wealth as nothing in comparison with her. (7:8).
Neither did I liken to her any priceless gem, because all gold is but a little sand in her sight, and silver will be accounted as clay before her. (7:9).
I loved her more than health and beauty, and I chose to have her rather than light because her radiance never ceases. (7:10).
All good things came to me along with her, and in her hands uncounted wealth. (7:11).
I rejoiced in them all because wisdom leads them, but I did not know that she was their mother. (7:12).
I learned without guile, and I impart without grudging; I do not hide her wealth, (7:13).
for it is an unfailing treasure for mortals; those who get it obtain friendship with God, commended for the gifts that come from instruction. (7:14).
May God grant me to speak with judgment and to have thoughts worthy of what I have received, for he is the guide even of wisdom and the corrector of the wise. (7:15).
For both we and our words are in his hand, as are all understanding and skill in crafts. (7:16).
For it is he who gave me unerring knowledge of what exists, to know the structure of the world and the activity of the elements, (7:17).
the beginning and end and middle of times, the alternations of the solstices and the changes of the seasons, (7:18).
the cycles of the year and the constellations of the stars, (7:19).
the natures of animals and the tempers of wild animals, the powers of spirits and the thoughts of human beings, the varieties of plants and the virtues of roots; (7:20).
I learned both what is secret and what is manifest, (7:21).

for wisdom, the fashioner of all things, taught me. There is in her a spirit that is intelligent, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, agile, clear, unpolluted, distinct, invulnerable, loving the good, keen, (7:22).
irresistible, beneficent, humane, steadfast, sure, free from anxiety, all-powerful, overseeing all, and penetrating through all spirits that are intelligent, pure, and altogether subtle. (7:23).
For wisdom is more mobile than any motion; because of her pureness she pervades and penetrates all things. (7:24).
For she is a breath of the power of God and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; therefore nothing defiled gains entrance into her. (7:25).
For she is a reflection of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. (7:26).

Although she is but one, she can do all things, and while remaining in herself, she renews all things; in every generation she passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets, (7:27).
for God loves nothing so much as the person who lives with wisdom. (7:28).
She is more beautiful than the sun and excels every constellation of the stars. Compared with the light she is found to be more radiant, (7:29).
for it is succeeded by the night, but against wisdom evil does not prevail. (7:30).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 3:5-12: Solomon asks for an understanding mind and God grants it.
1 Kings 4:29-33: Solomon speaks of trees, animals, birds, reptiles, and fish.
Job 28:12-19: Wisdom cannot be bought with gold or weighed out in silver.
Hebrews 1:3: The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact imprint of His nature.

translationNotes.note: Ancient reckoning counted pregnancy in lunar months of about 29 or 30 days, which spans roughly nine of our calendar months. Greek and Roman writers regularly say ten months for a full term.
Strips of cloth wound tightly around a newborn's body and limbs, the standard first care for an infant across the ancient Mediterranean. Ezekiel 16:4 and Luke 2:7 both mention the practice.
Dynamis here means potency or effective power. The virtue of a root is the medicinal strength of the plant, what a physician could draw out of it, not a moral quality.
A shining forth from a light source, the beam thrown off by the sun or a lamp rather than a second, separate flame. Hebrews 1:3 is the only place the word appears in the New Testament.

stories.keyTakeaway: Born mortal like everyone else, Solomon says kings enter and leave life the same way. He prayed and the spirit of wisdom came to him; through her he learned the structure of the world, the seasons, the stars, animals, and plants, and he calls her a breath of God's power and a spotless mirror.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 8
summaryBullets: She reaches mightily from one end of the earth to the other, and she orders all things well. (8:1).
I loved her and sought her from my youth; I desired to take her for my bride and became enamored of her beauty. (8:2).
She glorifies her noble birth by living with God, and the Lord of all loves her. (8:3).
For she is an initiate in the knowledge of God and an associate in his works. (8:4).
If riches are a desirable possession in life, what is richer than wisdom, the active cause of all things? (8:5).
And if understanding is effective, who more than she is fashioner of what exists? (8:6).
And if anyone loves righteousness, her labors are virtues, for she teaches self-control and prudence, justice and courage; nothing in life is more profitable for mortals than these. (8:7).

And if anyone longs for wide experience, she knows the things of old and infers the things to come; she understands turns of speech and the solutions of riddles; she has foreknowledge of signs and wonders and of the outcome of seasons and times. (8:8).
Therefore I determined to take her to live with me, knowing that she would give me good counsel and encouragement in cares and grief. (8:9).
Because of her I shall have glory among the multitudes and honor in the presence of the elders, though I am young. (8:10).
I shall be found keen in judgment, and in the sight of rulers I shall be admired. (8:11).
When I am silent they will wait for me, and when I speak they will give heed; if I speak at greater length, they will put their hands on their mouths. (8:12).
Because of her I shall have immortality and leave an everlasting remembrance to those who come after me. (8:13).
I shall govern peoples, and nations will be subject to me; (8:14).
dread monarchs will be afraid of me when they hear of me; among the people I shall show myself capable and courageous in war. (8:15).
When I enter my house, I shall find rest with her, for companionship with her has no bitterness, and life with her has no pain but gladness and joy. (8:16).
When I considered these things inwardly and pondered in my heart that in kinship with wisdom there is immortality, (8:17).

and in friendship with her, pure delight, and in the labors of her hands, unfailing wealth, and in the experience of her company, understanding, and renown in sharing her words, I went about seeking how to get her for myself. (8:18).
As a child I was naturally gifted, and a good soul fell to my lot, (8:19).
or rather, being good, I entered an undefiled body. (8:20).

But I perceived that I would not possess wisdom unless God gave her to me— and it was a mark of insight to know whose gift she was— so I appealed to the Lord and implored him, and with my whole heart I said, (8:21).
crossRefs: Proverbs 4:6-9: Love wisdom and she will guard you; embrace her and she will honor you.
Proverbs 7:4: Say to wisdom, You are my sister, and call insight your intimate friend.
1 Kings 10:1-3: The queen of Sheba tests Solomon with hard questions and he answers them all.
Job 29:9-10: Princes refrained from talking and laid their hand on their mouth.

translationNotes.term: self-control and prudence, justice and courage
translationNotes.note: The standard four-virtue list taught in the Greek schools. Sophrosyne is mastery of appetite, phronesis is practical good sense, dikaiosyne is giving each his due, andreia is courage under danger.

translationNotes.term: an initiate in the knowledge of God
translationNotes.note: A mystis was a woman admitted to a mystery cult and taught what outsiders were forbidden to hear. The book borrows that familiar Greek vocabulary to describe knowledge shared with God.
An ainigma is a saying framed to be hard, put to another as a test of wit. Samson's riddle in Judges 14 is the biblical example, and English enigma comes from the word.

translationNotes.term: put their hands on their mouths
translationNotes.original: Greek: χεῖρα ἐπιθήσουσιν ἐπὶ στόμα (cheira epithesousin epi stoma)
translationNotes.note: A recognized gesture of deference: the hearer covers his mouth to show he will not interrupt or answer back. Job 29:9 and 40:4 describe the same act.

stories.keyTakeaway: Solomon says wisdom reaches from one end of the earth to the other, and that he sought her from youth and desired her as his bride. She teaches self-control, prudence, justice, and courage, knows the past, infers the future, and solves riddles. He admits she is God's gift alone and turns to prayer.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 9
summaryBullets: “O God of my ancestors and Lord of mercy, who have made all things by your word (9:1).
and by your wisdom have formed humankind to have dominion over the creatures you have made (9:2).
and rule the world in holiness and righteousness and pronounce judgment in uprightness of soul, (9:3).
give me the wisdom that sits by your throne, and do not reject me from among your children. (9:4).
For I am your servant, the son of your female servant, a man who is weak and short-lived, with little understanding of judgment and laws, (9:5).
for even one who is perfect among humans will be regarded as nothing without the wisdom that comes from you. (9:6).
You have chosen me to be king of your people and to be judge over your sons and daughters. (9:7).
You have given command to build a temple on your holy mountain and an altar in the city of your habitation, a copy of the holy tent that you prepared from the beginning. (9:8).
With you is wisdom, she who knows your works and was present when you made the world; she understands what is pleasing in your sight and what is right according to your commandments. (9:9).
Send her forth from the holy heavens, and from the throne of your glory send her, that she may labor at my side and that I may learn what is pleasing to you. (9:10).
For she knows and understands all things, and she will guide me wisely in my actions and guard me with her glory. (9:11).
Then my works will be acceptable, and I shall judge your people justly and shall be worthy of the throne of my father. (9:12).
For who can learn the counsel of God? Or who can discern what the Lord wills? (9:13).
For the reasoning of mortals is worthless, and our designs are likely to fail, (9:14).
for a perishable body weighs down the soul, and this earthy tent burdens the thoughtful mind. (9:15).
We can hardly guess at what is on earth, and what is at hand we find with labor, but who has traced out what is in the heavens? (9:16).
Who has learned your counsel unless you have given wisdom and sent your holy spirit from on high? (9:17).
And thus the paths of those on earth were set right, and people were taught what pleases you and were saved by wisdom.” (9:18).
crossRefs: 2 Chronicles 1:8-10: Solomon asks God for wisdom and knowledge to govern this people.
Genesis 1:26-28: Humanity is given dominion over the creatures God has made.
Exodus 25:40: Make them according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.
Proverbs 8:27-30: Wisdom was there when God established the heavens.
2 Corinthians 5:1-4: The earthly tent we live in, and the groaning while we are in it.

translationNotes.note: Logos covers a spoken word, an account, and a reasoned plan behind an action. It is the word used for God's speech at creation in the Greek text of Genesis 1.

translationNotes.term: a copy of the holy tent
translationNotes.original: Greek: μίμημα σκηνῆς ἁγίας (mimema skenes hagias)
translationNotes.note: A mimema is a made copy that reproduces a pattern. Exodus 25:40 tells Moses to build the tabernacle according to the pattern shown him on the mountain.
A tent or booth, here used of the body as a temporary shelter that is pitched and struck. Paul uses the same image for the body in 2 Corinthians 5:1-4.

translationNotes.term: the son of your female servant
translationNotes.original: Greek: υἱὸς παιδίσκης σου (huios paidiskes sou)
translationNotes.note: A set phrase of self-abasement before a superior. The speaker claims a place in the household while taking the lowest rank in it; Psalm 116:16 uses the same formula.

stories.keyTakeaway: Solomon prays to the God of his ancestors, who made all things by his word, asking for the wisdom that sits beside God's throne. He calls himself a weak, short-lived servant chosen as king and judge and told to build a temple copying the holy tent, and asks that wisdom be sent down from heaven.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 10
summaryBullets: Wisdom protected the first-formed father of the world, when he alone had been created; she delivered him from his transgression (10:1).
and gave him strength to rule all things. (10:2).
But when an unrighteous man departed from her in his anger, he perished because in rage he killed his brother. (10:3).
When the earth was flooded because of him, wisdom again saved it, steering the righteous man by a paltry piece of wood. (10:4).

Wisdom also, when the nations in wicked agreement had been put to confusion, recognized the righteous man and preserved him blameless before God and kept him strong in the face of his compassion for his child. (10:5).
Wisdom rescued a righteous man when the ungodly were perishing; he escaped the fire that descended on the Five Cities. (10:6).
Evidence of their wickedness still remains: a continually smoking wasteland, plants bearing fruit that does not ripen, and a pillar of salt standing as a monument to an unbelieving soul. (10:7).

For because they passed wisdom by, they not only were hindered from recognizing the good but also left for humankind a reminder of their folly, so that their failures could never go unnoticed. (10:8).
Wisdom rescued from troubles those who served her. (10:9).

When a righteous man fled from his brother’s wrath, she guided him on straight paths; she showed him the kingdom of God and gave him knowledge of holy things; she prospered him in his labors and increased the fruit of his toil. (10:10).
When his oppressors were covetous, she stood by him and made him rich. (10:11).

She protected him from his enemies and kept him safe from those who lay in wait for him; in his arduous contest she declared him victorious, so that he might learn that godliness is more powerful than anything else. (10:12).
When a righteous man was sold, wisdom did not desert him but delivered him from sin. (10:13).

She descended with him into the dungeon, and when he was in prison she did not leave him, until she brought him the scepter of a kingdom and authority over his masters. Those who accused him she showed to be false, and she gave him everlasting honor. (10:14).
Holy people and blameless offspring wisdom delivered from a nation of oppressors. (10:15).
She entered the soul of a servant of the Lord and withstood dread kings with wonders and signs. (10:16).
She gave to holy people the reward of their labors; she guided them along a marvelous way and became a shelter to them by day and a starry flame through the night. (10:17).
She brought them over the Red Sea and led them through deep waters, (10:18).
but she drowned their enemies and cast them up from the depth of the sea. (10:19).
Therefore the righteous plundered the ungodly; they sang hymns, O Lord, to your holy name and praised with one accord your defending hand, (10:20).
for wisdom opened the mouths of those who were mute and made the tongues of infants speak clearly. (10:21).
crossRefs: Genesis 4:8: Cain rises against his brother Abel in the field and kills him.
Genesis 19:24-26: Fire falls on the cities of the plain and Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt.
Genesis 39:20-23: Joseph is put in the prison and the Lord is with him there.
Exodus 13:21: A pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night to give them light.
Exodus 14:26-28: The sea returns and covers the chariots and the horsemen.

translationNotes.term: the first-formed father of the world
translationNotes.original: Greek: πρωτόπλαστος πατὴρ κόσμου (protoplastos pater kosmou)
translationNotes.note: Protoplastos means first molded, from plasso, to shape clay, matching Genesis 2:7. This chapter names none of its figures, identifying each one only by what he did or suffered.
A standard Greek term for a group of five cities under one description. Genesis 14:2 names the five of the plain: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela, which is Zoar.
Xylon means cut timber, a plank or beam, not a living tree. Euteles means cheap, of trifling value, so the phrase stresses how slight the thing was that carried a man through the water.

translationNotes.original: Greek: τέρατα καὶ σημεῖα (terata kai semeia)
translationNotes.note: A fixed pair in the Greek Old Testament for the acts done in Egypt. A teras is a portent that startles the onlooker; a semeion is a sign that points beyond itself to its sender.

stories.keyTakeaway: Wisdom runs through the generations: she guarded the first-formed father, saw an angry man kill his brother, steered a righteous man through the flood on a plank, pulled one from the fire on the Five Cities, went to prison with the man who was sold, and brought a holy people through the Red Sea.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 11
summaryBullets: Wisdom prospered their works by the hand of a holy prophet. (11:1).
They journeyed through an uninhabited wilderness and pitched their tents in untrodden places. (11:2).
They withstood their enemies and fought off their foes. (11:3).
When they were thirsty, they called upon you, and water was given them out of flinty rock and from hard stone a remedy for their thirst. (11:4).
For through the very things by which their enemies were punished, they themselves received benefit in their need. (11:5).
Instead of the fountain of an ever-flowing river, stirred up and defiled with blood (11:6).
in rebuke for the decree to kill the infants, you gave them abundant water unexpectedly, (11:7).
showing by their thirst at that time how you punished their enemies. (11:8).
For when they were tried, though they were being disciplined in mercy, they learned how the ungodly were tormented when judged in wrath. (11:9).
For you tested them as a parent does in warning, but you examined the ungodly as a stern king does in condemnation. (11:10).
Whether absent or present, they were equally distressed, (11:11).
for a twofold grief possessed them and a groaning at the memory of what had occurred. (11:12).
For when they heard that through their own punishments the righteous had received benefit, they perceived it was the Lord’s doing. (11:13).

For though they had mockingly rejected him who long before had been cast out and exposed, at the end of the events they marveled at him, when they felt thirst in a different way from the righteous. (11:14).

In return for their foolish and wicked thoughts, which led them astray to worship irrational serpents and worthless animals, you sent upon them a multitude of irrational creatures to punish them, (11:15).
so that they might learn that one is punished by the very things by which one sins. (11:16).
For your all-powerful hand, which created the world out of formless matter, did not lack the means to send upon them a multitude of bears or bold lions (11:17).
or newly created unknown beasts full of rage or such as breathe out fiery breath or belch forth a thick pall of smoke or flash terrible sparks from their eyes; (11:18).
not only could the harm they did destroy people, but the mere sight of them could kill by fright. (11:19).

Even apart from these, people could fall at a single breath when pursued by justice and scattered by the breath of your power. But you have arranged all things by measure and number and weight. (11:20).
For it is always in your power to show great strength, and who can withstand the might of your arm? (11:21).
Because the whole world before you is like a speck that tips the scales and like a drop of morning dew that falls on the ground. (11:22).
But you are merciful to all, for you can do all things, and you overlook people’s sins, so that they may repent. (11:23).
For you love all things that exist and detest none of the things that you have made, for you would not have formed anything if you had hated it. (11:24).
How would anything have endured if you had not willed it? Or how would anything not called forth by you have been preserved? (11:25).
You spare all things, for they are yours, O Lord, you who love the living. (11:26).
crossRefs: Exodus 17:6: Moses strikes the rock at Horeb and water comes out for the people to drink.
Exodus 7:20-21: The water of the Nile turns to blood and the fish in it die.
Exodus 1:22: Pharaoh commands that every son born be thrown into the river.
Exodus 2:3-10: The child is set among the reeds and drawn out of the water.
Romans 2:4: God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance.

translationNotes.term: by measure and number and weight
translationNotes.original: Greek: μέτρῳ καὶ ἀριθμῷ καὶ σταθμῷ (metro kai arithmo kai stathmo)
translationNotes.note: The three ways goods were reckoned in a market: metron is a measure of volume, arithmos is a count of items, stathmos is a weight set on a balance. The phrase names ordinary commercial exactness.

translationNotes.term: a speck that tips the scales
translationNotes.original: Greek: ῥοπὴ ἐκ πλαστίγγων (rhope ek plastingon)
translationNotes.note: The plastinx is the pan of a balance, and the rhope is the least amount that makes the beam tip. The picture is the tiny added weight that decides a transaction at the scales.
Hyle first meant timber or raw stuff, and in Greek natural philosophy it named the unshaped material a craftsman works on. Amorphos means without form or outline.

Alogos means without logos, lacking speech and reason. It is the ordinary Greek adjective for a beast as distinct from a person, and it is used twice here of the creatures and the thinking behind their worship.

stories.keyTakeaway: Led by a holy prophet, the people cross untrodden wilderness and drink from flinty rock, while their enemies' river ran with blood over the decree to kill infants. God punishes the ungodly by the creatures they worshiped, orders all by measure, number, and weight, and spares all so they may repent.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 12
summaryBullets: For your immortal spirit is in all things. (12:1).

Therefore you correct little by little those who trespass, and you remind and warn them of the things through which they sin, so that they may be freed from wickedness and put their trust in you, O Lord. (12:2).
Those who lived long ago in your holy land (12:3).
you hated for their detestable practices, their works of sorcery and unholy rites, (12:4).
their merciless slaughter of children, and their sacrificial feasting on human flesh and blood. These initiates from the midst of a bloody revelry, (12:5).
these parents who murder helpless lives, you willed to destroy by the hands of our ancestors, (12:6).
so that the land most precious of all to you might receive a worthy colony of the children of God. (12:7).
But even these you spared, since they were but mortals, and sent wasps as forerunners of your army to destroy them little by little, (12:8).
though you were not unable to give the ungodly into the hands of the righteous in battle or to destroy them at one blow by dread wild animals or your stern word. (12:9).

But judging them little by little you gave them an opportunity to repent, though you were not unaware that their origin was evil and their wickedness inborn and that their way of thinking would never change. (12:10).
For their offspring were accursed from the beginning, and it was not through fear of anyone that you left them unpunished for their sins. (12:11).

For who will say, “What have you done?” or will resist your judgment? Who will accuse you for the destruction of nations that you made? Or who will come before you to plead as an advocate for the unrighteous? (12:12).
For neither is there any god besides you whose care is for all people, to whom you should prove that you have not judged unjustly, (12:13).
nor can any king or monarch confront you about those whom you have punished. (12:14).
You are righteous, and you rule all things righteously, deeming it alien to your power to condemn anyone who does not deserve to be punished. (12:15).
For your strength is the source of righteousness, and your sovereignty over all causes you to spare all. (12:16).
For you show your strength when people doubt the completeness of your power, and you rebuke any insolence among those who know it. (12:17).
Although you are sovereign in strength, you judge fairly, and with great forbearance you govern us, for you have power to act whenever you choose. (12:18).
Through such works you have taught your people that the righteous must be kind, and you have filled your children with good hope, because you give repentance for sins. (12:19).
For if you punished with such great care and indulgence the enemies of your children and those deserving of death, granting them time and opportunity to give up their wickedness, (12:20).
with what strictness you have judged your children, to whose ancestors you gave oaths and covenants full of good promises! (12:21).
So while chastening us you scourge our enemies ten thousand times more, so that when we judge we may meditate upon your goodness, and when we are judged we may expect mercy. (12:22).
Therefore those who lived unrighteously, in a life of folly, you tormented through their own abominations. (12:23).
For they went far astray on the paths of error, accepting as gods those animals that even their enemies despised; they were deceived like foolish infants. (12:24).
Therefore, as though to children who cannot reason, you sent your judgment to mock them. (12:25).
But those who have not heeded the warning of mild rebukes will experience the deserved judgment of God. (12:26).

For when in their suffering they became incensed at those creatures that they had thought to be gods, being punished by means of them, they saw and recognized as the true God the one whom they had before refused to know. Therefore the utmost condemnation came upon them. (12:27).
crossRefs: Exodus 23:28: I will send the hornet before you to drive out the inhabitants of the land.
Deuteronomy 18:9-12: The detestable practices of the nations, sorcery and passing children through fire.
Leviticus 18:24-25: The land became defiled and vomited out its inhabitants.
Romans 9:20: A human being has no standing to answer back to God.
2 Peter 3:9: The Lord is patient, not wanting any to perish but all to come to repentance.

translationNotes.note: Pharmakeia covers the mixing of drugs, potions, and spells, a trade practiced for hire. It shares a root with pharmakon, a compounded drug that could heal or kill depending on dose.
The same stinging-insect image used in the Greek text of Exodus 23:28 and Deuteronomy 7:20 for what goes ahead of Israel to drive the inhabitants out little by little.
An apoikia was a settlement planted away from the mother city, with citizens sent out to hold and work new land. The word describes a formal transfer of population, not a wandering camp.
From myrias, ten thousand, the largest named unit in Greek counting. Saying ten thousand times is the standard way to say beyond counting, not a precise multiple.

stories.keyTakeaway: God's immortal spirit fills all things, so he corrects little by little. The land's former inhabitants practiced sorcery, killed children, and ate human flesh, yet he sent wasps ahead of his army rather than destroy them at one blow, giving them room to repent and teaching his people to be kind.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 13
summaryBullets: For all people who were ignorant of God were foolish by nature, and they were unable from the good things that are seen to know the one who exists, nor did they recognize the artisan while paying heed to his works; (13:1).
but they supposed that either fire or wind or swift air or the circle of the stars or turbulent water or the luminaries of heaven were the gods that rule the world. (13:2).
If through delight in the beauty of these things people assumed them to be gods, let them know how much better than these is their Lord, for the author of beauty created them. (13:3).
And if people were amazed at their power and working, let them perceive from them how much more powerful is the one who formed them. (13:4).
For from the greatness and beauty of created things comes a corresponding perception of their Creator. (13:5).
Yet these people are little to be blamed, for perhaps they go astray while seeking God and desiring to find him. (13:6).
For while they live among his works, they keep searching and trust in what they see because the things that are seen are beautiful. (13:7).
Yet again, not even they are to be excused, (13:8).
for if they had the power to know so much that they could investigate the world, how did they not more quickly find the Lord of these things? (13:9).

But miserable, with their hopes set on dead things, are those who give the name “gods” to the works of human hands, gold and silver fashioned with skill and likenesses of animals or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand. (13:10).
A skilled woodcutter may saw down a tree easy to handle and skillfully strip off all its bark and then with pleasing workmanship make a useful vessel that serves life’s needs (13:11).
and burn the cast-off pieces of his work to prepare his food and eat his fill. (13:12).

But a cast-off piece from among them, useful for nothing, a stick crooked and full of knots, he takes and carves with care in his leisure and shapes it with skill gained in idleness; he forms it in the likeness of a human being (13:13).
or makes it like some worthless animal, giving it a coat of red paint and coloring its surface red and covering every blemish in it with paint; (13:14).
then he makes a suitable niche for it and sets it in the wall and fastens it there with iron. (13:15).
He takes thought for it so that it may not fall, because he knows that it cannot help itself, for it is only an image and has need of help. (13:16).
When he prays about possessions and his marriage and children, he is not ashamed to address a lifeless thing. For health he appeals to a thing that is weak; (13:17).
for life he prays to a thing that is dead; for aid he entreats a thing that is utterly inexperienced; for a prosperous journey, a thing that cannot take a step; (13:18).
for money-making and work and success with his hands, he asks strength of a thing whose hands have no strength. (13:19).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 4:19: Do not be drawn away to bow down to the sun, the moon, and the stars.
Psalm 19:1: The heavens declare the glory of God and the sky proclaims His handiwork.
Isaiah 44:14-17: A man cuts a tree, cooks with half of it, and bows to the rest as a god.
Jeremiah 10:3-5: The idol is fastened with hammer and nails so it will not totter.
Romans 1:20-23: God's power is seen in what He made, yet they exchanged His glory for images.

translationNotes.term: the artisan, the one who exists
translationNotes.original: Greek: τεχνίτης (technites) and ὁ ὤν (ho on)
translationNotes.note: A technites is a craftsman trained in a techne, a trade. Ho on, the one who is, is the phrase the Greek Old Testament uses at Exodus 3:14 for the name God gives Moses.

translationNotes.term: the circle of the stars and the luminaries of heaven
translationNotes.original: Greek: κύκλος ἄστρων (kyklos astron) and φωστῆρες (phosteres)
translationNotes.note: Phosteres, light-bearers, is the word used for the sun and moon in the Greek text of Genesis 1:14-16. The circle of the stars is the turning band of the night sky as it was described then.
Miltos is red ochre, an iron-rich earth pigment ground and mixed with a binder. It was the common finish for worked wood, ships' timbers, and carved figures across the Mediterranean.
Household and shrine images were set in a recess cut into the wall and pinned with iron cramps or nails, the same method masons used to hold stone blocks together.

stories.keyTakeaway: Those ignorant of God took fire, water, and the stars for the gods that rule the world, missing the Creator behind the beauty. Worse are those who call handmade things gods: a woodcutter burns his scraps to cook, carves a knotted leftover into a human shape, paints it red, and bolts it to the wall.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 14
summaryBullets: Again, one preparing to sail and about to voyage over raging waves calls upon a piece of wood more fragile than the ship that carries him. (14:1).
For it was desire for gain that planned that vessel, and wisdom was the artisan who built it, (14:2).
but it is your providence, O Father, that steers its course, because you have given it a path in the sea and a safe way through the waves, (14:3).
showing that you can save from every danger, so that even a person who lacks skill may put to sea. (14:4).

It is your will that works of your wisdom should not be without effect; therefore people trust their lives even to the smallest piece of wood, and passing through the billows on a raft they come safely to land. (14:5).
For even in the beginning, when arrogant giants were perishing, the hope of the world took refuge on a raft and guided by your hand left to the world the seed of a new generation. (14:6).
For blessed is the wood by which righteousness comes. (14:7).
But the idol made with hands is accursed, and so is the one who made it— he for having made it, and the perishable thing because it was named a god. (14:8).
For equally hateful to God are the ungodly and their ungodliness, (14:9).
for what was done will be punished together with the one who did it. (14:10).

Therefore there will be a visitation also upon the idols of the nations, because, though part of what God created, they became an abomination, stumbling blocks for human souls and a trap for the feet of the foolish. (14:11).
For the idea of making idols was the beginning of sexual immorality, and the invention of them was the corruption of life, (14:12).
for they did not exist from the beginning, nor will they last forever. (14:13).
For through human vanity they entered the world, and therefore their speedy end has been planned. (14:14).

For a father, consumed with grief at an untimely bereavement, made an image of his child, who had been suddenly taken from him; he now honored as a god what was once a dead human being and handed on to his dependents secret rites and initiations. (14:15).
Then the ungodly custom, grown strong with time, was kept as a law, and at the command of monarchs carved images were worshiped. (14:16).

When people could not honor monarchs in their presence, since they lived at a distance, they imagined their appearance far away and made a visible image of the king whom they honored, so that by their zeal they might flatter the absent one as though present. (14:17).
Then the ambition of the artisan impelled even those who did not know the king to intensify their worship. (14:18).
For he, perhaps wishing to please his ruler, skillfully forced the likeness to take more beautiful form, (14:19).
and the multitude, attracted by the charm of his work, now regarded as an object of worship the one whom shortly before they had honored as a human. (14:20).
And this became a hidden trap for humankind, because people, in bondage to misfortune or to royal authority, bestowed on objects of stone or wood the name that ought not to be shared. (14:21).
Then it was not enough for them to err about the knowledge of God, but though living in great strife due to ignorance, they call such great evils peace. (14:22).
For whether they kill children in their initiations or celebrate secret mysteries or hold frenzied revels with strange customs, (14:23).
they no longer keep either their lives or their marriages pure, but they either treacherously kill one another or grieve one another by adultery, (14:24).
and all is a raging riot of blood and murder, theft and deceit, corruption, faithlessness, tumult, perjury, (14:25).
confusion over what is good, forgetfulness of favors, defiling of souls, sexual perversion, disorder in marriages, adultery, and debauchery. (14:26).
For the worship of idols not to be named is the beginning and cause and end of every evil. (14:27).
For their worshipers either rave in exultation or prophesy lies or live unrighteously or readily commit perjury, (14:28).
for because they trust in lifeless idols they swear wicked oaths and expect to suffer no harm. (14:29).

But just penalties will overtake them on two counts: because they thought wrongly about God in devoting themselves to idols and because in deceit they swore unrighteously through contempt for holiness. (14:30).
For it is not the power of the things by which people swear but the just penalty for those who sin that always pursues the transgression of the unrighteous. (14:31).
crossRefs: Genesis 6:4: The giants were on the earth in those days.
Genesis 7:23: Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark.
Isaiah 44:9-11: All who make idols are nothing, and their craftsmen are put to shame.
Daniel 3:1-7: At the king's command all peoples bow down to the golden image he set up.
Romans 1:24-27: They exchanged the truth about God for a lie, and dishonoring followed.

translationNotes.note: Pronoia means forethought, seeing to a matter in advance. In Greek writing it was the standard term for the ordering care that governs the world; Acts 24:2 uses it of a governor's administration.
The Greek translators used gigantes, the word for the earth-born giants of Greek mythology, to render Hebrew nephilim and rephaim. The loan supplies the vocabulary only, not the Greek stories.

translationNotes.term: carved images worshiped at the command of monarchs
translationNotes.note: Glypta are things cut or carved. In the Hellenistic kingdoms cities set up statues of a distant ruler and voted him honors, sacrifices, and titles, which is the practice described here.

translationNotes.original: Greek: μυστήρια καὶ τελεταί (mysteria kai teletai)
translationNotes.note: Teletai were the initiation ceremonies of a closed cult and mysteria the things shown only to those admitted, under an oath of silence that made outsiders liable for disclosing them.

stories.keyTakeaway: A sailor trusts a fragile plank while God's providence steers the ship, as it steered the raft when the giants perished. Idols began when a grieving father made an image of his dead child and when subjects honored likenesses of absent kings; secret rites, murder, and perjury followed after them.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 15
summaryBullets: But you, our God, are kind and true, patient, and ruling all things in mercy. (15:1).
For even if we sin we are yours, knowing your power; but we will not sin because we know that you acknowledge us as yours. (15:2).
For to know you is complete righteousness, and to know your power is the root of immortality. (15:3).
For neither has the evil intent of human art misled us, nor the fruitless toil of painters, a figure stained with varied colors, (15:4).
whose appearance arouses yearning in fools, so that they desire the lifeless form of a dead image. (15:5).
Lovers of evil things and fit for such objects of hope are those who either make or desire or worship them. (15:6).

A potter kneads the soft earth and laboriously molds each vessel for our service, fashioning out of the same clay both the vessels that serve clean uses and those for contrary uses, making all alike, but which shall be the use of each of them the worker in clay decides. (15:7).

With misspent toil, these workers form a futile god from the same clay— these mortals who were made of earth a short time before and after a little while go to the earth from which all mortals are taken, when the time comes to return the souls that were borrowed. (15:8).

But the workers are not concerned that mortals are destined to die or that their life is brief, but they compete with workers in gold and silver and imitate workers in copper, and they count it a glorious thing to mold counterfeit gods. (15:9).
Their heart is ashes, their hope is cheaper than dirt, and their lives are of less worth than clay, (15:10).
because they failed to know the one who formed them and inspired them with active souls and breathed a living spirit into them. (15:11).
But they considered our existence an idle game and life a festival held for profit, for they say one must get money however one can, even by base means. (15:12).
For these persons, more than all others, know that they sin when they make from earthy matter fragile vessels and carved images. (15:13).
But most foolish and more miserable than an infant are all the enemies who oppressed your people. (15:14).

For they thought that all the idols of the nations were gods, though these have neither the use of their eyes to see with, nor nostrils with which to draw breath, nor ears with which to hear, nor fingers to feel with, and their feet are of no use for walking. (15:15).
For a human made them, and one whose spirit is borrowed formed them, for none can form gods that are like themselves. (15:16).
People are mortal, and what they make with lawless hands is dead, for they are better than the objects they worship, since they have life, but the idols never had. (15:17).
Moreover, they worship even the most hateful animals, which are worse than all others when judged by their lack of intelligence, (15:18).
and even as animals they are not so beautiful in appearance that one would desire them, but they have escaped both the praise of God and his blessing. (15:19).
crossRefs: Genesis 2:7: God forms the man from the dust and breathes into him the breath of life.
Jeremiah 18:3-6: The potter reworks the spoiled clay on his wheel into another vessel.
Isaiah 45:9: Woe to the one who quarrels with his Maker, clay against the potter.
Romans 9:21: From the same lump the potter makes one vessel for honor and another for common use.
Psalm 115:5-7: They have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, feet but do not walk.

translationNotes.term: a potter, the worker in clay
translationNotes.note: The kerameus threw wet clay on a wheel, and one shop turned out storage jars, cooking pots, lamps, and chamber vessels alike. Clean uses and contrary uses names the two ends of that same output.
Apaiteo is the verb for calling in a debt, demanding back what was lent. The image treats a life as a loan the lender may require at his own time; Luke 12:20 uses the same verb.
Chalkos is copper and its alloy bronze. English versions render it brass, bronze, or copper for the same metal, and casting figures in it was a separate trade from working gold and silver.

translationNotes.original: Greek: τὰ ἔχθιστα τῶν θηρίων (ta echthista ton therion)
translationNotes.note: Egyptian temples kept living animals as honored images of their gods: the Apis bull at Memphis, the crocodile of Sobek, the ibis of Thoth, the cat of Bastet, and sacred serpents, fed by priests and embalmed at death.

stories.keyTakeaway: God is kind, patient, and rules in mercy, and to know him is complete righteousness. A potter kneads one lump into vessels for clean and unclean uses, then molds a counterfeit god from the same clay. The oppressors took for gods images with no eyes, ears, or feet, and even the most hateful animals.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 16
summaryBullets: Therefore those people were deservedly punished through such creatures and were tormented by a multitude of animals. (16:1).
Instead of this punishment you showed kindness to your people, and you prepared quails to eat, a delicacy to satisfy the desire of appetite, (16:2).

in order that those people, when they desired food, might lose the least remnant of appetite because of the odious creatures sent to them, while your people, after suffering want a short time, might partake of delicacies. (16:3).
For it was necessary that upon those oppressors inescapable want should come, while to these others it was merely shown how their enemies were being tormented. (16:4).
For when the terrible rage of wild animals came upon your people and they were being destroyed by the bites of writhing serpents, your wrath did not continue to the end; (16:5).
they were troubled for a little while as a warning and received a symbol of deliverance to remind them of your law’s command. (16:6).
For the one who turned toward it was saved not by the thing that was beheld but by you, the Savior of all. (16:7).
And by this also you convinced our enemies that it is you who deliver from every evil. (16:8).
For they were killed by the bites of locusts and flies, and no healing was found for them because they deserved to be punished by such things. (16:9).
But your children were not conquered even by the fangs of venomous serpents, for your mercy came to their help and healed them. (16:10).
To remind them of your oracles they were bitten and then were quickly delivered, so that they would not fall into deep forgetfulness and become unresponsive to your kindness. (16:11).
For neither herb nor poultice cured them, but it was your word, O Lord, that heals all people. (16:12).
For you have power over life and death; you lead mortals down to the gates of Hades and back again. (16:13).
A person in wickedness kills another but cannot bring back the departed spirit or set free the imprisoned soul. (16:14).
To escape from your hand is impossible, (16:15).
for the ungodly, refusing to know you, were flogged by the strength of your arm, pursued by unusual rains and hail and relentless storms and utterly consumed by fire. (16:16).
For—most incredible of all—in water, which quenches all things, the fire had still greater effect, for the universe defends the righteous. (16:17).

At one time the flame was restrained, so that it might not consume the creatures sent against the ungodly, but that seeing this they might know that they were being pursued by the judgment of God, (16:18).
and at another time even in the midst of water it burned more intensely than fire, to destroy the crops of the unrighteous land. (16:19).
Instead of these things you gave your people food of angels, and without their toil you supplied them from heaven with bread ready to eat, providing every pleasure and suited to every taste. (16:20).
For your sustenance manifested your sweetness toward your children, and the bread, ministering to the desire of the one who took it, was changed to suit everyone’s liking. (16:21).

Snow and ice withstood fire without melting, so that they might know that the crops of their enemies were being destroyed by the fire that blazed in the hail and flashed in the showers of rain; (16:22).
whereas the fire, in order that the righteous might be fed, even forgot its native power. (16:23).
For creation, serving you who made it, exerts itself to punish the unrighteous and in kindness relaxes on behalf of those who trust in you. (16:24).
Therefore at that time also, changed into all forms, it served your all-nourishing bounty, according to the desire of those who had need, (16:25).
so that your children, whom you loved, O Lord, might learn that it is not the production of crops that feeds humankind but that your word sustains those who trust in you. (16:26).
For what was not destroyed by fire was melted when simply warmed by a fleeting ray of the sun, (16:27).
to make it known that one must rise before the sun to give you thanks and must pray to you at the dawning of the light, (16:28).
for the hope of an ungrateful person will melt like wintry frost and flow away like wastewater. (16:29).
crossRefs: Numbers 11:31-32: A wind brings quail in from the sea and they fall around the camp.
Numbers 21:6-9: Those bitten by the serpents look at the bronze serpent and live.
Exodus 9:23-25: Hail with fire flashing in it strikes down the crops of Egypt.
Exodus 16:14-15: A fine flaky substance lies on the ground and the people ask what it is.
Psalm 78:24-25: He rained down manna on them, and they ate the bread of angels.

translationNotes.note: The word used in the Greek text of Exodus 16:13, literally quail-mother. Migrating quail cross the Sinai in huge flocks and come down so spent that they can be gathered by hand.
A symbolon was a token: a seal, a broken tally, or a marked object that identified its holder or guaranteed an agreement. It stood for something beyond itself and had no power of its own.
A malagma was a softening plaster of oil, herbs, and resin spread on a wound or swelling. With botane, a medicinal plant, this names the two standard treatments a physician of the day would apply.
Psalm 78:25 in the Greek Old Testament calls the manna bread of angels. The phrase marks where the bread came from, sent down from heaven, and this chapter keeps the same wording.

stories.keyTakeaway: God's enemies are killed by locusts and flies with no cure, while his people, bitten by serpents, look at a symbol of deliverance and are healed by his word, not by herb or poultice. Fire and hail ruin the crops of the unrighteous, while his people eat bread of angels that suits every taste.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 17
summaryBullets: Great are your judgments and hard to describe; therefore uninstructed souls have gone astray. (17:1).

For when lawless people supposed that they held the holy nation in their power, they themselves lay as captives of darkness and prisoners of long night, shut in under their roofs, exiles from eternal providence. (17:2).
For thinking that in their secret sins they were unobserved behind a dark curtain of forgetfulness, they were scattered, terribly alarmed and appalled by specters. (17:3).
For not even the inner chamber that held them protected them from fear, but terrifying sounds rang out around them, and dismal phantoms with gloomy faces appeared. (17:4).
And no power of fire was able to give light, nor did the brilliant flames of the stars avail to illumine that hateful night. (17:5).
Nothing was shining through to them except a dreadful, self-kindled fire, and in terror they deemed the things that they saw to be worse than that unseen appearance. (17:6).
The delusions of their magic art lay humbled, and their boasted wisdom was scornfully rebuked. (17:7).
For those who promised to drive off the fears and disorders of a sick soul were sick themselves with ridiculous fear. (17:8).
For even if nothing disturbing frightened them, yet, scared by the passing of wild animals and the hissing of snakes (17:9).
they perished in trembling fear, refusing to look even at the air, though it nowhere could be avoided. (17:10).
For wickedness is a cowardly thing, condemned by its own testimony; distressed by conscience, it has always exaggerated the difficulties. (17:11).
For fear is nothing but a giving up of the helps that come from reason, (17:12).
and hope, being weaker, prefers ignorance of what causes the torment. (17:13).
But throughout the night, which was really powerless and which came upon them from the recesses of powerless Hades, they all slept the same sleep (17:14).
and now were driven by monstrous specters and now were paralyzed by their souls’ surrender, for sudden and unexpected fear overwhelmed them. (17:15).
And whoever was there fell down and thus was kept shut up in a prison not made of iron; (17:16).
for whether they were farmers or shepherds or workers who toiled in the wilderness, they were seized and endured the inescapable fate, for with one chain of darkness they all were bound. (17:17).
Whether there came a whistling wind, or a melodious sound of birds in wide-spreading branches, or the rhythm of violently rushing water, (17:18).

or the harsh crash of rocks hurled down, or the unseen running of leaping animals, or the sound of the most savage roaring beasts, or an echo thrown back from a hollow of the mountains, it paralyzed them with terror. (17:19).
For the whole world was illumined with brilliant light and went about its work unhindered, (17:20).
while over those people alone heavy night was spread, an image of the darkness that was destined to receive them, but still heavier than darkness were they to themselves. (17:21).
crossRefs: Exodus 10:21-23: A darkness that can be felt covers Egypt three days while Israel has light.
Exodus 7:11-12: Pharaoh's magicians do the same by their secret arts.
Proverbs 28:1: The wicked flee when no one pursues.
Job 18:5-11: The light of the wicked is put out and terrors startle him on every side.

translationNotes.note: The magoi were a priestly class among the Medes and Persians, and Greek borrowed the term for professionals who sold spells, omens, and ritual power. Techne marks it as a trade with a learned craft.
A phasma is an apparition, a thing that shows itself. The word covers dream images, shapes seen at night, and portents in the sky, all of them read at the time as warnings.
Syneidesis means knowing together with oneself, the awareness a person carries of his own acts, standing as a witness against him. Romans 2:15 uses the same word.
Automatos means happening of itself with no outside cause, the root of English automatic. A pyra was a heaped fire built up for burning, so the phrase names a blaze that no one lit.

stories.keyTakeaway: The captors of the holy nation lie shut under their roofs as prisoners of a long night, scattered by specters and terrified by sounds they cannot see. Their magic arts are humbled, and farmers, shepherds, and laborers alike are bound by one chain of darkness while the whole world stands in light.
