stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 18
summaryBullets: But for your holy ones there was very great light. Their enemies heard their voices but did not see their forms and counted them happy for not having suffered (18:1).
and were thankful that your holy ones, though previously wronged, were doing them no injury, and they begged their pardon for having been at variance with them. (18:2).
Therefore you provided a flaming pillar of fire as a guide for your people’s unknown journey and a harmless sun for their glorious wandering. (18:3).

For their enemies deserved to be deprived of light and imprisoned in darkness, those who had kept your children imprisoned, through whom the imperishable light of the law was to be given to the world. (18:4).

When they had resolved to kill the infants of your holy ones, and one child had been abandoned and rescued, you in punishment took away a multitude of their children, and you destroyed them all together by a mighty flood. (18:5).
That night was made known beforehand to our ancestors so that they might rejoice in sure knowledge of the oaths in which they trusted. (18:6).
The deliverance of the righteous and the destruction of their enemies were expected by your people. (18:7).
For by the same means by which you punished our enemies you called us to yourself and glorified us. (18:8).

For in secret the holy children of good people offered sacrifices and with one accord agreed to the divine law, so that the holy ones would share alike the same things, both blessings and dangers, and already they were singing the praises of the ancestors. (18:9).
But the discordant cry of their enemies echoed back, and their piteous lament for their children was spread abroad. (18:10).
The slave was punished with the same penalty as the master, and the commoner suffered the same loss as the king, (18:11).

and they all together by the one form of death had corpses too many to count. For the living were not sufficient even to bury them, since in one instant their most valued children had been destroyed. (18:12).
For though they had disbelieved everything because of their magic arts, yet when their firstborn were destroyed they acknowledged your people to be God’s child. (18:13).
For while gentle silence enveloped all things and night in its swift course was now half-gone, (18:14).
your all-powerful word leaped from heaven, from the royal throne, into the midst of the land that was doomed, a stern warrior (18:15).
carrying the sharp sword of your authentic command, and stood and filled all things with death and touched heaven while standing on the earth. (18:16).
Then at once apparitions in dreadful dreams greatly troubled them, and unexpected fears assailed them, (18:17).
and one here and another there, hurled down half-dead, made known why they were dying, (18:18).
for the dreams that disturbed them forewarned them of this, so that they might not perish without knowing why they suffered. (18:19).
The experience of death touched also the righteous, and a plague came upon the multitude in the desert, but the wrath did not long continue. (18:20).

For a blameless man was quick to act as their champion; he brought forward the shield of his ministry, prayer and propitiation by incense; he withstood the anger and put an end to the disaster, showing that he was your servant. (18:21).
He conquered the wrath not by strength of body, not by force of arms, but by his word he subdued the avenger, appealing to the oaths and covenants given to our ancestors. (18:22).
For when the dead had already fallen on one another in heaps, he intervened and held back the assault and cut off its way to the living. (18:23).
For on his long robe the whole world was depicted, and the glories of the ancestors were engraved on the four rows of stones, and your majesty was on the diadem upon his head. (18:24).
To these the destroyer yielded, these he feared, for merely to test the wrath was enough. (18:25).
crossRefs: Exodus 12:6-13: The lamb killed at twilight and the blood put on the doorposts.
Exodus 12:29-30: At midnight the firstborn die, from Pharaoh's to the captive's, and a great cry rises.
Exodus 13:21-22: The pillar of fire by night gives them light so they can travel.
Numbers 16:46-48: Aaron runs with a censer, stands between the dead and the living, and the plague stops.
Exodus 28:17-21: Four rows of engraved stones set in the high priest's breastpiece.

translationNotes.term: night in its swift course was now half-gone
translationNotes.note: The night was reckoned in watches, and its midpoint was a fixed marker rather than a clock reading. Half-gone night is midnight, the hour named in Exodus 12:29.
A compounded incense burned on coals in a censer. Numbers 16:46-48 describes a priest carrying a censer out into the camp and standing with it between the dead and the living.

Poderes means reaching to the feet, the term the Greek Old Testament uses for the high priest's full-length robe. Exodus 28 sets twelve engraved stones in four rows on his breastpiece and a gold plate on his turban.
The participle used in the Greek text of Exodus 12:23 for the one who strikes. Hebrews 11:28 and 1 Corinthians 10:10 carry the same word over into the New Testament.

stories.keyTakeaway: His holy ones have great light and a pillar of fire while their captors have none. On the night made known beforehand, God's all-powerful word leaps from heaven as a stern warrior and fills the land with death; slave and king lose their firstborn. A blameless man halts a plague with incense.

stories.title: 📜 Wisdom of Solomon 19
summaryBullets: But the ungodly were assailed to the end by pitiless anger, for God knew in advance even their future actions: (19:1).
how, though they themselves had permitted your people to depart and hastily sent them out, they would change their minds and pursue them. (19:2).

For while they were still engaged in mourning and were lamenting at the graves of their dead, they reached another foolish decision and pursued as fugitives those whom they had begged and compelled to leave. (19:3).
For the fate they deserved drew them on to this end and made them forget what had happened, in order that they might fill up the punishment that their torments still lacked (19:4).
and that your people might experience an incredible journey, but they themselves might meet a strange death. (19:5).
For the whole creation in its nature was fashioned anew, complying with your commands, so that your children might be kept unharmed. (19:6).
The cloud was seen overshadowing the camp and dry land emerging where water had stood before, an unhindered way out of the Red Sea and a grassy plain out of the raging waves, (19:7).
where those protected by your hand passed through as one nation, after gazing on marvelous wonders. (19:8).
For they ranged like horses and leaped like lambs, praising you, O Lord, who delivered them. (19:9).
For they still recalled the events of their sojourn, how instead of producing animals the earth brought forth gnats, and instead of fish the river spewed out vast numbers of frogs. (19:10).
Afterward they saw also a new kind of bird, when desire led them to ask for luxurious food, (19:11).
for, to give them relief, quails came up from the sea. (19:12).

The punishments did not come upon the sinners without prior signs in the violence of thunder, for they justly suffered because of their wicked acts, for they practiced a more bitter hatred of strangers. (19:13).
Others had refused to receive strangers when they came to them, but these made slaves of guests who were their benefactors. (19:14).
And not only so, but while punishment of some sort will come upon the former for having received strangers with hostility, (19:15).
the latter, having first received them with festal celebrations, afterward afflicted with terrible sufferings those who had already shared the same rights. (19:16).

They were stricken also with loss of sight— just as were those at the door of the righteous man— when, surrounded by yawning darkness, all of them tried to find the way through their own doors. (19:17).

For the elements changed places with one another, as on a harp the notes vary the nature of the rhythm, while each note remains the same. This may be clearly inferred from the sight of what took place. (19:18).
For land animals were transformed into water creatures, and creatures that swim moved over to the land. (19:19).
Fire even in water retained its normal power, and water forgot its fire-quenching nature. (19:20).
Flames, on the contrary, failed to consume the flesh of perishable creatures that walked among them, nor did they melt the crystalline, quick-melting kind of heavenly food. (19:21).
For in everything, O Lord, you have exalted and glorified your people, and you have not neglected to help them at all times and in all places. (19:22).
crossRefs: Exodus 14:5-9: Pharaoh changes his mind and pursues the people he had sent away.
Exodus 8:1-6: The river swarms with frogs that come up over the whole land.
Exodus 8:16-17: The dust of the earth becomes gnats throughout Egypt.
Genesis 19:11: The men at Lot's door are struck blind and grope to find the entrance.
Exodus 15:1-2: Israel sings to the Lord after passing through the sea.

translationNotes.note: Stoicheia were the four basic constituents of the world in Greek natural science: earth, water, air, and fire, each with its own place and behavior. The same word also means the letters that make up a written line.

translationNotes.term: as on a harp the notes vary the rhythm
translationNotes.note: A stringed instrument plucked with the fingers rather than struck. Retuning the same set of strings changes the pattern that is heard while each individual string keeps its own note.

translationNotes.term: a more bitter hatred of strangers
translationNotes.original: Greek: μισοξενία (misoxenia), the opposite of φιλοξενία (philoxenia)
translationNotes.note: Philoxenia, love of strangers, was the recognized duty of a host to take in a traveler, feed him, and guarantee his safety. Misoxenia names the refusal of that duty; Hebrews 13:2 commands the first.
Krystalloeides means ice-like in appearance. Exodus 16:14 describes the manna as fine and flaky like frost on the ground, and Exodus 16:21 says it melted once the sun grew hot.

stories.keyTakeaway: The enemy changes its mind and pursues the people it begged to leave, still mourning its dead. Creation is refashioned: dry land and a grassy plain rise in the sea, and the nation crosses as one, praising God. Those who enslaved their guests go blind; the elements change places like notes on a harp.

intro:
The Wisdom of Solomon speaks in Solomon's voice from first chapter to last. The speaker addresses the rulers and judges of the earth (1:1; 6:1-11) and tells God, "You have chosen me to be king of your people and to be judge over your sons and daughters. You have given command to build a temple on your holy mountain and an altar in the city of your habitation" (9:7-8). He says he was born mortal like everyone else, molded in the womb and nursed in swaddling cloths, since no king has a different beginning of existence (7:1-6), and that he prayed and the spirit of wisdom came to him, and he preferred her to scepters and thrones (7:7-8). Those are the marks of Solomon son of David, who reigned over Israel from about 970 to 931 BC, asked at Gibeon for a discerning heart (1 Kings 3:5-14), and built the temple in Jerusalem (1 Kings 6-8). The Greek manuscripts head the book with his name: Sophia Salomonos (Σοφία Σαλωμῶνος), the Wisdom of Solomon.

The book signs no line of its own, and the early church did not settle on a single account of how a book of Solomon came to stand in Greek. The Greek is the book's own language rather than a rendering of a Hebrew original, and that is the point on which the ancient discussion turned. Several proposals were made within Bible-affirming tradition. (1) Solomon: the plain sense of the speaker's claims and of the title carried by the Greek codices, and the reckoning of the Latin West, which counted five books of Solomon (Salomonis libri quinque) at the Council of Hippo (AD 393) and the Councils of Carthage (AD 397 and 419), the five being Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Wisdom, and Ecclesiasticus. (2) Friends of Solomon writing in his honour: the Muratorian Canon (c. AD 170-200), the oldest surviving list of its kind, calls it Wisdom "written by the friends of Solomon in his honour." (3) Philo of Alexandria: Jerome reports in his Preface to the Books of Solomon (c. AD 398) that "some of the ancient scribes affirm this one is of Philo Judaeus." Jerome's own judgment there was that the book "was never among the Hebrews, the very style of which reeks of Greek eloquence," and he retitled it Liber Sapientiae, the Book of Wisdom, which is why many editions print it simply as Wisdom. (4) Jesus son of Sirach: Augustine wrote in On Christian Doctrine 2.8 (c. AD 397) that Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus "are ascribed to Solomon from a certain resemblance of style, but the most likely opinion is that they were written by Jesus the son of Sirach"; in his Retractations he withdrew that, judging it more probable that Sirach did not write this book. City of God 17.20 gives his summary of the question: the Western church had long received the book, and the ascription to Solomon rested on resemblance of style.

On the first reading the date is Solomon's reign, about 970 to 931 BC. On the others the Greek text belongs to Greek-speaking Judaism, and the sustained attention to living animals kept as gods in temples (15:18-19) points to Egypt; the Muratorian Canon shows the book in Christian use before the end of the second century AD. It runs in three movements. Chapters 1 through 6 address kings and judges, declare that God did not make death (1:13), and set out the reasoning of the ungodly who plot a shameful death for the righteous man who calls God his father (2:1-20). Chapters 7 through 9 are the king's account of how he came by wisdom, closing in the prayer of chapter 9. Chapters 10 through 19 retell the history from the first man to the crossing of the sea and name no person in it. Every figure is identified by act or circumstance: the first-formed father of the world (10:1), the man who killed his brother in rage (10:3), the one steered through the flood by a paltry piece of wood (10:4), the man who was sold and went down into the dungeon (10:13-14), a holy prophet (11:1). Places keep their names where people do not: the Five Cities (10:6), the Red Sea (10:18; 19:7). Set inside the retelling is a long excursus on idolatry (13:1-15:19) covering the worship of fire, wind, stars, and water, the woodcutter who carves a knotted offcut into a human shape and fastens it in a wall niche with iron (13:11-15), and the grieving father who made an image of his dead child (14:15).

The vocabulary is that of the Greek schools turned to the book's own use: athanasia (ἀθανασία), deathlessness, at 3:4 and 8:17; aphtharsia (ἀφθαρσία), incorruption, at 2:23 and 6:18-19; pronoia (πρόνοια), the forethought that orders the world, at 14:3 and 17:2; the four cardinal virtues of the philosophers listed together at 8:7; and apaugasma (ἀπαύγασμα), the radiance thrown off a light source, at 7:26, a word the New Testament uses once, at Hebrews 1:3. In the Septuagint codices Wisdom stands with the books of Solomon, and the Vulgate places it between Song of Songs and Ecclesiasticus; its oldest witnesses are Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, and Alexandrinus (fourth and fifth centuries AD). Athanasius, in Festal Letter 39 (AD 367), set it outside his canon list but among the books appointed by the fathers to be read to those just approaching. The Council of Trent (Fourth Session, 8 April 1546) named Sapientia in its decree on the canonical Scriptures, and the Eastern churches receive it among the books read in church; the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England (Article VI, 1563) list it among the books read "for example of life and instruction of manners." In the Roman rite chapter 3, verses 1 to 9, on the souls of the righteous in the hand of God, is among the standard readings at funerals.
